prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

From the ninth-century Irish poem Pangur Bán and I at work, Adepts, equals, cat and clerk: His whole instinct is to hunt, Mine to free the meaning pent. More than loud acclaim, I love Books, silence, thought, my alcove. Happy for me, Pangur Bán Child-plays round some mouse’s den. Truth to tell, just being here, Housed alone, housed together, Adds up to its own reward: Concentration, stealthy art. Next thing an unwary mouse Bares his flank: Pangur pounces. Next thing lines that held and held Meaning back begin to yield. All the while, his round bright eye Fixes on the wall, while I Focus my less piercing gaze On the challenge of the page. With his unsheathed, perfect nails Pangur springs, exults and kills. When the longed-for, difficult Answers come, I too exult. So it goes. To each his own. No vying. No vexation. Taking pleasure, taking pains, Kindred spirits, veterans. Day and night, soft purr, soft pad, Pangur Bán has learned his trade. Day and night, my own hard work Solves the cruxes, makes a mark.

outputs.L1:
From the ninth-century Irish poem *Pangur Bán*:

*Pangur Bán* and I at work:  
Adepts, equals—cat and clerk.  
His whole instinct is to hunt;  
Mine, to free the meaning pent.  

More than loud acclaim, I love  
Books, silence, thought, my alcove.  
Happy for me, Pangur Bán  
Child-plays round some mouse’s den.  

Truth to tell, just being here,  
Housed alone, housed together,  
Adds up to its own reward:  
Concentration, stealthy art.  

Next thing, an unwary mouse  
Bares his flank: Pangur pounces.  
Next thing, lines that held and held  
Meaning back begin to yield.  

All the while, his round bright eye  
Fixes on the wall, while I  
Focus my less piercing gaze  
On the challenge of the page.  

With his unsheathed, perfect nails,  
Pangur springs, exults, and kills.  
When the longed-for, difficult  
Answers come, I too exult.  

So it goes. To each his own.  
No vying. No vexation.  
Taking pleasure, taking pains,  
Kindred spirits, veterans.  

Day and night, soft purr, soft pad,  
Pangur Bán has learned his trade.  
Day and night, my own hard work  
Solves the cruxes, makes a mark.
outputs.L2:
From the ninth-century Irish poem:

Pangur Bán and I labor side by side—  
skilled companions, matched in purpose,  
he the cat, I the scholar.  
All his nature drives him toward the chase;  
mine is bent on releasing meanings held fast.

I prize books, quiet, reflection,  
and my small room  
more than the roar of public praise.  
It is happiness enough for me  
that Pangur Bán plays like a kitten  
beside some mouse’s hiding place.

In truth, simply being here—  
alone, yet sharing the same dwelling—  
is reward in itself:  
my deep attention,  
his secretive craft.

Soon, some careless mouse  
exposes its side,  
and Pangur leaps.  
Soon, too, the lines that long resisted me  
begin to give up the sense  
they had kept enclosed.

All the while,  
his bright, rounded eye  
stares toward the wall,  
as I turn my duller sight  
to the difficulty of the written page.

With flawless claws drawn bare,  
Pangur springs forward,  
triumphs, and kills.  
And when the hard-won answers  
I have desired at last arrive,  
I also rejoice.

That is how our lives proceed:  
each of us has his proper task.  
There is no rivalry,  
no irritation.  
We take both pleasure and trouble in our work—  
two kindred spirits,  
seasoned in our crafts.

By day and night,  
with quiet purr and gentle tread,  
Pangur Bán has mastered his profession.  
By day and night,  
my own demanding labor  
untangles hard problems  
and leaves its sign behind.
outputs.L3:
The speaker compares his scholarly work with Pangur Bán’s instinctive hunting, showing how both activities require patience, attention, and skill. While the clerk searches through books and wrestles with difficult meanings, the cat quietly watches for mice and waits for the right moment to strike. Although their tasks are very different, each is absorbed in a craft that feels natural and satisfying.

Both Pangur Bán and the clerk find happiness in practicing their own separate forms of work. The cat is content when he succeeds in catching his prey, just as the scholar feels joy when he finally understands a challenging text or solves an intellectual problem. Their achievements may seem small, but the poem presents them as deeply meaningful because they come from focused effort and personal dedication.

The poem also celebrates quiet solitude, concentration, and companionship. The scholar and the cat do not need to disturb one another; instead, they share the same peaceful space while each pursues his own purpose. This creates a gentle sense of harmony, as their separate activities exist side by side. The companionship between them is not loud or dramatic, but calm and respectful.

Pangur Bán’s success in catching mice parallels the speaker’s joy in uncovering difficult meanings. Just as the cat’s patience is rewarded when he catches a mouse, the scholar’s persistence is rewarded when he reaches understanding. In this way, the poem suggests that intellectual labor and physical instinct can be equally valuable and fulfilling.

Overall, the cat and the scholar are presented as kindred spirits. Both take pleasure in patient, skilled work, and both are happiest when they are free to follow their own nature. Through this comparison, the poem honors the quiet rewards of concentration, companionship, and devotion to one’s craft.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a quiet scene of companionship between a scholar and his cat, Pangur Bán. Both are shown at work in the same room, each absorbed in a different but parallel task. The cat hunts mice, watching carefully and waiting for the right moment to strike, while the scholar studies his books, searching patiently for meaning and understanding. Although their activities seem different, the poem shows that they require similar qualities: focus, skill, patience, and persistence.

Pangur Bán takes pleasure in his own craft, stalking and catching mice with alert attention. In the same way, the scholar finds satisfaction in intellectual pursuit, reading, thinking, and discovering truths hidden in texts. Neither figure is idle, and neither interferes with the other. Instead, they work side by side in peaceful harmony, each content with his own purpose. The cat’s success comes when he catches his prey, while the scholar’s success comes when he grasps a difficult idea or solves a problem in his studies.

The poem suggests that fulfillment does not always come from grand achievements or public recognition. It can be found in ordinary, disciplined labor done well. Both the scholar and the cat experience joy because they are fully engaged in what they are made to do. Their work is private and quiet, but it is meaningful to them. The poem also emphasizes companionship without competition. The scholar does not envy the cat, and the cat does not disturb the scholar; instead, their shared dedication creates a sense of mutual respect and calm.

Through this comparison, the poem celebrates the pleasures of concentration and purposeful activity. It shows that the life of the mind and the instinctive life of an animal can mirror each other in surprising ways. Pangur Bán and the scholar are united by their commitment to their separate tasks, and the poem finds beauty in that simple parallel. In the end, it portrays work not as a burden, but as a source of quiet happiness, independence, and companionship.
outputs.L5:
From Irish tradition comes the charming figure of **Pangur**, often remembered as **Pangur Bán**, the white cat in a medieval poem written by an Irish monk. The poem beautifully compares the monk’s quiet search for knowledge with Pangur’s patient hunt for mice. Both are focused, both work in silence, and both find joy in their own tasks.

This small piece of Irish literature has lasted for centuries because it feels simple and human. Pangur is not just a cat; he becomes a symbol of companionship, concentration, and peaceful daily life. From a distant Irish monastery to modern readers around the world, Pangur continues to remind us that happiness can be found in humble work and quiet moments.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a modern English verse translation of the ninth-century Irish poem “Pangur Bán,” preserving the parallel between the scholar and his cat.
counterfactuals.output:
**Pangur Bán**

Pangur Bán, my little white cat,  
and I keep each to our own craft:  
he sets his mind on hunting mice,  
I set mine on hunting words.

Better than praise, better than noise,  
we sit together, glad and still;  
each of us finds in his own art  
a private joy, a practiced skill.

When Pangur crouches by the wall,  
bright-eyed, intent on one small hole,  
I bend above my book and page,  
to catch a meaning with my soul.

Often a mouse, by leap and claw,  
is taken in his silent snare;  
often a difficult line grows clear,  
and I rejoice to find it there.

He has his game, he has his gift:  
his paw is quick, his gaze is keen.  
I have my pen, my lamp, my thought,  
and trace what hidden words may mean.

So in one room, by night and day,  
we work without envy or blame:  
Pangur Bán at his delight,  
and I at mine—we love the same.

He hunts the shadow for a mouse;  
I hunt the dark for truth and light.  
Each finds, when patient labor wins,  
his own reward, his own delight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you produce a poetic adaptation of “Pangur Bán” in the style of Seamus Heaney, beginning with “Pangur Bán and I at work”?
counterfactuals.output:
Pangur Bán and I at work,  
each of us lodged in his own luck:  
his white paw testing the shadowed floor,  
my black ink nosing a line for more.

The lamp-hush gathers. Outside, rain  
frets at the thatch and leaves again.  
Inside, the vellum’s pale hide gleams;  
a mouse-thought stirs in Pangur’s dreams.

He has his craft, the sudden spring,  
the narrowed eye, the pounce, the fling;  
I have my quarry, word by word,  
a meaning netted, a silence stirred.

Often he pads from chair to sill,  
tail like a question, body still,  
then strikes—clean joy in claw and bone—  
and brings his small dark triumph home.

So I, bent close, will track and wait  
through briar of gloss and thorn of date,  
until, from under Latin’s stone,  
some bright sense scuttles out alone.

No envy here, no lordly rod:  
just two lean servants under God,  
pleased by the task our natures chose—  
his moonlit hunt, my ink-black rows.

And when the dawn begins to spill  
its milk along the window-sill,  
Pangur blinks, and I look up:  
both of us fed from the same cup.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a lyrical translation of the medieval Irish poem about the monk and his white cat, emphasizing study, solitude, and the cat hunting mice.
counterfactuals.output:
**Pangur Bán — a lyrical rendering**

I and my white cat, Pangur Bán,  
keep house alone, apart from men;  
he hunts the darting mouse by night,  
I hunt the word by candlelight.

Better than praise or feast or fame  
is each of us at his own game:  
his paw poised still beside the wall,  
my mind bent close above the scroll.

When some small shadow stirs the floor,  
his bright eyes kindle, asking more;  
when some hard meaning yields to me,  
my heart leaps up as wild and free.

So in our quiet cell we stay,  
two scholars in our separate way:  
he with his claws and moon-white fur,  
I with my pen, a patient seeker.

No envy troubles either art;  
each has his craft, each has his part.  
Pangur takes mice in silent flight,  
I take dark thoughts and turn them light.

Thus gladly through the hours we fare,  
alone together, pair by pair:  
my book, his hunt; his chase, my lore—  
and peace comes padding on the floor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhymed poem based on “Pangur Bán,” where a scholar compares his search for meaning in books to his cat’s hunt for prey.
counterfactuals.output:
At midnight’s desk I trim my light,  
While Pangur pads the floor;  
I stalk a thought through thickets white,  
He hunts beside the door.  

My quarry hides in ink and gloss,  
In margins faint and thin;  
His flickers past the rushes’ moss,  
A whisker, tail, and skin.  

I set my snare with patient eyes,  
A question, line by line;  
He crouches low where shadow lies,  
And makes the darkness shine.  

No envy stirs between our trades,  
No boast, no bitter plea;  
He loves the pounce the silence aids,  
I love the mind set free.  

When from the page a meaning springs,  
Bright as a mouse from grass,  
He leaps; I catch my hidden things  
In words that come to pass.  

So scholar, cat, and candle flame  
Keep watch till night is done:  
Two hunters, differing but the same,  
Who find our joy in one.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Recreate the poem “Pangur Bán” as a polished contemporary English poem with short lines, quiet imagery, and the theme “to each his own.”
counterfactuals.output:
**Pangur Bán**

Pangur, white cat,  
keeps his own watch.

I keep mine  
over the page.

He hunts the mouse  
in the hush of the room;

I hunt a thought  
through the dark of a line.

His eye is bright  
at the wall’s small stirring.

Mine bends close  
to a difficult word.

He is glad  
when claws close true.

I am glad  
when meaning comes clear.

No envy between us,  
no need to trade.

He has his craft,  
and I have mine.

All night we work  
by the same small lamp:

Pangur with patience,  
silent and quick;

I with my books,  
slow and still.

When morning finds us,  
each has his prize—

a mouse in the corner,  
a verse in the mind.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
